### [Taking the PULSE of Enterprise Workflows: Evaluating Persistent Project-State Understanding](<https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.28374>)

PULSE evaluates whether enterprise agents can reconstruct what remains open, what changed, and which updates a collaborator has encountered across time-stamped project records. On synthetic enterprise histories, controlled evidence and project-state interventions expose separate retrieval and state-reconciliation failures, giving builders a targeted way to evaluate persistent understanding before relying on it for coordination.

PULSE extends existing synthetic HERB histories with 1,573 questions over 30 projects: 779 open-loop, 563 evolution and 231 documented-view questions. With GPT-5.6-Sol in the controlled ReAct setup, macro-averaged extraction F1 is 31.4, compared with 52.9 for full pre-cutoff context, 66.9 for gold source artifacts and 78.1 when the same artifacts are supplemented with resolved project state. **Limitations:** HERB histories are synthetic and follow fixed workflows; 19 validation gates and selected state rules do not establish real-enterprise label validity. ### [STUN-Bench: Truly Unseen Tools for Evaluating Shared Tool Experience](<https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.30034>)

STUN-Bench excludes held-out tools from shared experience and retriever training, then shows how pooling other tools' experience can crowd their descriptions out of candidate retrieval. Its leakage audit, matched exposure controls and conditional separate-index mitigation help builders evaluate shared tool memory more faithfully, while the measured outcome remains tool routing rather than successful API execution.

**Limitations:** Unseen means excluded from shared experience and clean-retriever training, not absent from base-model pretraining. ## [2026-11-15](../../../reports/2026/11/2026-11-15.md) — PARTIAL SEARCH

### [CapLite: Prompt-Injection Defense for Small Language Model Agents without Model-Written Security Artifacts](<https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.17115>)

CapLite commits write operations before reading tool results and uses deterministic schema rules to admit sensitive arguments only when grounded in the user request. This separates a small model's proposals from authorization: the authors report no successful tool-goal attacks in 13,935 AgentDojo episodes across 15 models. The protection trades away task utility and leaves final answers and free-text payloads unprotected, so it is a scoped write-control design rather than complete prompt-injection immunity.

Eight-model robustness tests add tool-knowledge, read-exfiltration and descriptor-collision attacks; mediator and write-commitment ablations admit attacks. ### [Termination Lag: Coding Agents Solve Early but Stop Late](<https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.14960>)

The researchers record every distinct intermediate repository patch and test it offline to measure how long coding agents continue after first producing a benchmark-correct fix. The resulting termination-lag metrics reveal verification effort and occasional regressions hidden by final solve rates, providing a reference for evaluating stopping policies. The analysis uses an oracle available only after execution and does not show that the measured steps can safely be removed in deployment.

No author code/project or earlier public artifact was verified.

**Limitations:** One run per task, no repeated-seed intervals, and success is defined only by the official benchmark tests. Offline first-correct stopping is an oracle reference, not a learned deployable rule; necessary verification may have broader value outside those tests. Steps approximate effort and do not directly measure wall-clock, monetary, token or energy savings. Tool/argument rules label activities; step/context limits terminate 1-4% of solved runs, and Seed-OSS solves few Pro tasks. ## [2026-10-13](../../../reports/2026/10/2026-10-13.md) — PARTIAL SEARCH

### [AgentSWE: Can Coding Agents Build the Agent You Actually Want?](<https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.13361>)

AgentSWE tests whether coding agents can create, edit and optimize the agents users request, freezing each delivery before running it on held-out cases derived from the requirements. Its 25 commissions expose a gap between convincing development demonstrations and working delivered behavior, giving builders a concrete evaluation for overfitting, incomplete runtimes and unsupported completion claims.

**Published:** 2026-10-09 · **First seen:** 2026-10-15T04:39:34.000Z · **Novelty:** newly-discovered · **Tags:** Agent Construction, Held-Out Evaluation, Requirement Fidelity

**Public availability:** 2026-10-12T00:00:00Z (inferred from dated announcement and official schedule). [Timing source](<https://arxiv.org/list/cs.AI/recent?skip=0&show=2000>) · [Timing source](<https://info.arxiv.org/help/availability.html>)

[Paper](<https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.13361>) · [Code](<https://github.com/VectorSpaceLab/AgentSWE>)

**Evidence:** research-paper; full-text. Delayed discovery from the October 12 batch; original submission was October 9 at 10:35:27 UTC. Sections 3–5 and Appendix J distinguish requirement rubrics, hard validity gates, development/held-out splits and model/harness pairings. Main Creation results average 11.2/100 over 50 builds; 20 score zero. The code and 25-task package are accessible, and source history begins October 12 at 02:05:44 UTC, within the discovery lookback.

**Limitations:** Main model/task pairings were built once; an eight-task subset uses three builds and shows large variation. Creation/Editing rely on model judges whose model families overlap some builders, and absolute scores across task families and Lite/main settings are not directly comparable. Public held-out assets and builder network access leave contamination risks; no experiments were reproduced.

## [2026-10-12](../../../reports/2026/10/2026-10-12.md) — PARTIAL SEARCH

### [VEPA: Verified Evolving Formal Policy for Lifelong LLM Agent Guardrails](<https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.12813>)

VEPA uses a language model to propose symbolic guardrail updates, then checks rule structure and conflicts before granting supported rules permission to make deterministic decisions on parsed events. This separates policy learning from enforcement and improves the reported safety-versus-overrefusal tradeoff as feedback accumulates, while uncovered events require a separate fallback.

**Published:** 2026-10-08 · **First seen:** 2026-10-12T10:03:40Z · **Novelty:** new · **Tags:** Agent Guardrails, Formal Policies, Online Adaptation

**Public availability:** 2026-10-12T00:00:00Z (inferred from dated announcement and official schedule). [Timing source](<https://arxiv.org/list/cs.AI/new>) · [Timing source](<https://info.arxiv.org/help/availability.html>)

[Paper](<https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.12813>)

**Evidence:** research-paper; full-text. Sections 3–5 and Appendices B–F specify search, evidence gating and five-seed prequential evaluation. On the same covered examples, final macro-F1 is 0.81 on ASSEBench-Safety and 0.76 on ATBench, exceeding the strongest baselines by 0.02 and 0.09; active coverage is approximately 80% and 88%. October 12 NEW item 12 plus the official Sunday schedule supports inferred public availability, preserving the October 8 submission date.

**Limitations:** Recorded trajectory streams do not test live behavioral feedback. Guarantees apply only after neural parsing and within a fixed schema, excluding fallback. The default posterior median gate reuses policy-selection data and is neither selection-adjusted nor time-uniform assurance. No author code was verified; results were not reproduced.

### [TRACE: Diagnosing Verifier Brittleness in Agentic Evaluation](<https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.11678>)

TRACE's new experiments test whether agent score changes survive repeated runs and whether different judges evaluate the same behavior consistently. These controls help separate behavioral regressions, ordinary run variation and changes in what the evaluator rewards.

**Published:** 2026-10-08 · **First seen:** 2026-10-09T10:11:06Z · **Novelty:** material-update · **Tags:** Agent Evaluation, Verifier Diagnostics, Replication

[Paper](<https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.11678>) · [Code](<https://github.com/RGaonkar/trace-verifier-stress-tests>)

**Evidence:** research-paper; full-text. Sections 5 and Appendix E add four-agent replication with 88 fresh tasks. Seven of eight presentation-change comparisons meet a prespecified ±0.10 equivalence margin; misleading-name controls reduce reward for all four agents.

**Limitations:** Equivalence permits effects below that margin; missingness is nonrandom and native reward is not ground truth. The public repository contains older synthetic/July diagnostics; parity with the new replication artifacts was not verified. Results were not reproduced.

**Update:** 2026-10-09: the newly announced arXiv report adds repeated four-agent replication and a two-judge audit beyond the August 2 public framework's July 28 single-model diagnostic. The paper's original October 8 submission date is retained. ## [2026-10-09](../../../reports/2026/10/2026-10-09.md) — PARTIAL SEARCH

### [On the estimation and validity of AI time horizons—a statistical look at the METR plot](<https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.12466>)

This statistical audit re-estimates METR's software-task time horizons with shared monotone splines and item-response models, testing predictions by holding out entire task families. It finds that equal multipliers in human task duration can represent different capability gains, providing diagnostics for interpreting agent progress without treating a single horizon number as a universal capability scale.

**Published:** 2026-10-08 · **First seen:** 2026-10-09T10:05:00Z · **Novelty:** new · **Tags:** Agent Evaluation, Construct Validity, Item Response Theory

**Public availability:** 2026-10-09T00:00:00Z (inferred from dated announcement and official schedule). [Timing source](<https://arxiv.org/list/cs.AI/new>) · [Timing source](<https://info.arxiv.org/help/availability.html>)

[Paper](<https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.12466>)

**Evidence:** research-paper; full-text. Sections 2–3 and Appendix A analyze 228 software tasks, 79 families and 26 AIs. Five-fold family-level validation crosses four proper scoring rules with three task/family weightings; both proposed models have better pooled point estimates than shared-slope logistic regression on all 12 metrics. Figures 1 and 4 identify a relatively flat human-time-to-difficulty mapping around 2–30 minutes.

**Limitations:** This is a reanalysis of one task suite, not a new agent or an independent capability benchmark. Most per-AI intervals remain wide. The audit assumes task representativeness and annotation validity, and does not overturn the empirical exponential trend. A horizon refers to human completion time, not AI runtime; no author code artifact was verified.

## [2026-10-07](../../../reports/2026/10/2026-10-07.md) — PARTIAL SEARCH

### [Agent in a Bottle: Can LLM Agents Turn Their Capabilities Into Cheap, Scalable Artifacts?](<https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.08775>)

BOTTLED tests whether an agent can build and apply a reusable program or smaller model to an entire unlabeled workload under fixed time and API budgets. It measures the practical ability to turn expensive per-example competence into an economical batch solution, revealing failures that ordinary zero-shot accuracy misses.

**Published:** 2026-10-06 · **First seen:** 2026-10-07T10:05:04Z · **Novelty:** new · **Tags:** Agent Evaluation, Reusable Artifacts, Amortized Cost

**Public availability:** 2026-10-07T00:00:00Z (inferred from dated announcement and official schedule). [Timing source](<https://arxiv.org/list/cs.AI/recent>) · [Timing source](<https://info.arxiv.org/help/availability.html>)

[Paper](<https://arxiv.org/html/2610.08775v1>) · [Code](<https://github.com/aktsonthalia/bottled>)

**Evidence:** research-paper; full-text. Across ten models, three tasks and two runs per setting, 31 of 60 agent runs underperform the stronger of two small-model distillation baselines with the same weighted-token budget. A populated public repository provides the harness, budget enforcement, datasets scripts and baselines.

**Limitations:** Only three narrow NLP workloads and one harness are evaluated. Zero-shot scores and full-workload costs are estimated from 1,000 examples, while bottled predictions cover the full workload. Equal token budgets do not mean identical monetary or compute budgets, and contamination checking uses an agentic judge.

### [AgentDojo: A Dynamic Environment to Evaluate Prompt Injection Attacks and Defenses for LLM Agents](<https://arxiv.org/abs/2406.13352>)

AgentDojo provides an extensible environment for testing whether tool-using agents complete legitimate tasks while resisting instructions embedded in untrusted tool results. It makes the security-versus-utility tradeoff measurable and supplies reusable tasks, attack surfaces, and defense baselines for agent evaluations.

**Published:** 2024-06-19 · **First seen:** 2026-09-30T04:13:56.564Z · **Novelty:** baseline · **Tags:** Prompt Injection, Evaluation, Tool Use

**Positioning:** open-reference

[Paper](<https://arxiv.org/abs/2406.13352>) · [Code](<https://github.com/ethz-spylab/agentdojo>)

**Evidence:** research-paper; full-text. The paper defines user and attacker goals across 97 tasks and 629 security test cases and evaluates defenses, including tool filtering. The accessible repository supports extension; arXiv records June 19, 2024 for v1 and November 24, 2024 for the inspected v3.

**Limitations:** The original scores concern historical models and the included environments, not current deployment security. Tool filtering can fail when required tools also enable an attack; the original suite does not cover continuing user tasks with an unreset context.

### [Failure-Transparent Agents: Benchmarking Post-Failure Reporting in Tool-Using Language Models](<https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.35732>)

Failure-Transparent Agents isolates a reporting problem by giving models fixed failed-tool traces and checking whether subsequent claims are supported by the available evidence. Its structured evidence contract offers a concrete design to test when reducing false completion claims, while preserving useful recovery advice.

**Published:** 2026-09-28 · **First seen:** 2026-09-30T04:13:56.564Z · **Novelty:** baseline · **Tags:** Evaluation, Reliability, Evidence

**Positioning:** frontier-research

[Paper](<https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.35732>)

**Evidence:** research-paper; full-text. The benchmark includes 100 synthetic blocked tasks and 3,600 human-annotated responses across six models; authors report pooled false-success rates of 22.8% for baseline and 0.8% with the contract. Submission history verifies September 28, 2026 at 17:51:41 UTC.

**Limitations:** A new preprint measuring response fidelity after fixed failures, not end-to-end execution or recovery. The contract bundles multiple changes, the additional model cohort is post-confirmatory, and independent double annotation or inter-annotator agreement is not reported.
